# Landscape metrics and fragments {#lagoa-landscape}

The metrics in this chapter are computed on the original map grid, without
reprojection. Areas and edges are measured on the ellipsoid, and there is no
need to specify a UTM zone.

## Metrics per year {-}

`biomastats_metrics()` reclassifies the maps to the classes of interest and,
year by year, computes area, edges, number of fragments and the aggregation
index. Let us follow the forest formation:

```{r metrics, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.width=6, fig.height=4.5}
metrics <- biomastats_metrics(maps, classes = 3, metrics = "keep.all")
metrics$ai_plot
metrics$fragments_number
```

```{r include=FALSE}
mt <- metrics$metrics_table
m85 <- mt[mt$Year == 1985, ]; m24 <- mt[mt$Year == 2024, ]
```

Besides shrinking, the forest became more fragmented: the number of fragments
went from `r m85[["Number of Fragments"]]` to `r m24[["Number of Fragments"]]`,
and the aggregation index fell from `r num(m85[["Aggregation Index (%)"]], 0)`% to
`r num(m24[["Aggregation Index (%)"]], 0)`%. The full table is in
`metrics$metrics_table`; for a single map, use `lulc_metrics()`.

`reclass_map()` highlights the selected class against the rest of the
landscape:

```{r reclassified, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", fig.width=6, fig.height=5.5}
reclass_map(metrics, year = 1985)
reclass_map(metrics, year = 2024)
```

## Fragments {-}

`fragment_metrics()` goes down to the level of each fragment. For every one, it
measures area, perimeter, core area, shape, fractal dimension, centroid,
elongation and distance to the nearest neighbour; for each class and year, it
summarises the size distribution:

```{r fragments, fig.height=5.5}
fragments <- fragment_metrics(maps, classes = 3, years = c(1985, 2004, 2024),
                              language = "en")
fragments$plots$map
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
s <- fragments$summary
tabela(data.frame(Year = s$year, Fragments = s$n_patches, `Area (ha)` = s$class_area_ha,
                  `Mean area (ha)` = s$area_mean, `Median area (ha)` = s$area_median,
                  `Largest fragment (% of landscape)` = s$lpi, Gini = s$area_gini,
                  `Nearest neighbour, median (m)` = s$enn_median, check.names = FALSE), 2)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
s85 <- s[s$year == 1985, ]; s24 <- s[s$year == 2024, ]
```

The average fragment shrank from `r num(s85$area_mean, 1)` ha to
`r num(s24$area_mean, 1)` ha, and the largest one, which covered
`r num(s85$lpi, 1)`% of the landscape, now covers `r num(s24$lpi, 1)`%. Size
inequality (Gini) remains high, meaning that a few fragments hold most of the
forest. The data for each fragment are in `fragments$patches`.
